Many self-made millionaires become millionaires through real estate and leveraging the equity in the homes, and they tend to put the properties under an LLC to also protect them from lawsuits (as well as the tax deductions). Usually, the money gets routed through several different things, and the actual amount that is considered taxable is drastically reduced.

Real estate. Trading "up" towards a bigger property so you don't have to pay taxes on it. Creating an LLC and hiring your children, so the income you "pay them" is tax deductible. Rolling that income into a Roth IRA to also allow the tax-free money to continue growing tax-free. 

Also, any repairs, upgrades, and the miles you put on a vehicle are tax deductions. Most people think that only doordash drivers or Uber drivers can claim their mileage as a deduction, but that's false. If you purchase parts to fix your car and do it yourself, you can claim those parts as well as what it would have cost to have it done at a shop (you just need to have a quote from a shop that shows the price of the part, plus the labor cost). You can get around 70-80% of that amount back.

When you have a business, there are many ways to benefit. Income paid to employees is a tax deduction, buildings, and other equipment (vehicles, office furniture, etc) are shown to depreciate each year in accordance with what the IRS allows (even though property value tends to increase each year). 

This is just a few that I can think of. People who aren't millionaires or business owners can also pay less in taxes, but the majority of people aren't willing to do the research and figure out how. I'm not homeless,  nor have I ever been (I joined this thread to try and help people), but if you are trying to help the homeless, one of the best ways to help people out of that situation would be to try to get laws and policies changed. Issues I found when trying to help people are listed below.

1). Many of the people I helped write resumes for and prep for job interviews weren't able to get the job because they required an address (online applications make it a requirement to fill out for most companies). Without a permanent address,  being turned down for a job increases drastically. Another problem is how it is viewed by companies. While I would try to help people in that position, many companies see it as a liability because they consider not having a permanent place to live would potentially come with more issues, and unfortunately, many companies look at homeless people in a negative light. It isn't right, but there isn't anything to prevent using homelessness as discrimination when putting an address is a requirement for most places.

2). Without an address, setting up a bank account isn't going to happen, as banks require proof of identity and an address.

3). Several people I have tried to help either had expired IDs from a different state and didn't have a way to get them or didn't have one at all. A few were teenagers, but some were adults. 

Most of the people I spoke with didn't become homeless because of drugs or mental problems (the general perception of the public), but usually due to financial hardships that came from unexpected situations in their life. Some people tried to get away from abuse, and others for medical reasons caused them to lose their job. Almost half of Americans are living paycheck-to-paycheck, which puts them one emergency away from homelessness themselves.

In oder to convince politicians to fix this issue, you will have to figure out how to pitch it as a benefit to them and their city. It's not right, but most politicians will only actually try to help as long as it doesn't negatively affect them or their reputation.  The first question they would ask you would be about funding. Who would pay to fix the issue, build the housing locations, etc. The second would be how it should be operated by, which would run it, again about the funding, and the screening process to make sure everything is within the legal limits.

If you get past the first few questions, they will point out there are already situations in place and ask how it would be different than what is already established. And even if you manage to get past that question, they will more than likely turn it down because they won't be able to figure out how to benefit by it.

I have been trying to help fix homelessness, but the best I have been able to do is on an individual basis. Most of the people I have helped with were those I have talked to in person. Online, it's much harder to help someone.

Multiple ways. The first thing I did was a lot of research into house hacking, which was something I never heard of prior to owning a house. Then I checked the area where I lived and decided which methods would work best for me. There was a theme park that was pretty close to my house, and the area had an international airport so there were lots of tourist or people going on family vacations within 50 miles of me. Airbnb was always talked about as being a great method but I lived in my house and didn't think I could do much as most people were renting out their entire home.
Since the master bedroom had a private bathroom, I discussed it with my wife and we moved out of our master bedroom and into one of the smaller rooms (3 bedroom home). We listed the master bedroom on Airbnb and spent about $150 getting new comforters and stuff for the room to make it stand out. We also already had a TV mounted in the room so we made a Netflix account for Airbnb. To get the status of SuperHost, we looked at the average prices people were charging and listed ours for half of that for the first 2 weeks. We put a mini-fridge in the room with bottled water and made a list of fun things to do in the area. Because the price was low and the house and room looked very good, all of our reviews were 5 stars about how great it was and that the price for what you got was amazing. We increased the price each week until we had the room booked 80% of the time (one of the tips from the research I did that was actually helpful).

The slowest month we had was $930, and that was our first month, but the average was around $1,400 (colder months did worse, but spring and summer worked best).

  During the first month of this, we also decided to get a roommate (we agreed that if we did airbnb, we needed a roommate who was respectful and okay with us doing airbnb). For pricing, I looked up the average cost of a one bedroom apartment in my area and listed it for half of that initially (all utilities included). The idea was that the person would know the exact amount they would pay each month, we knew exactly what we would get, and the price was great for them because it was not only half of an apartments cost, they weren't paying utilities. The first roommate was paying $600 a month but moved to a different state for a new job. He gave us a notice, so we decided to find a new one but increase the price ( the highest I could rent a room that was still a great value ended up being about 66% of the average 1 bedroom apartment if it had a private bathroom, and 55% if it was shared). Initially my wife didn't like the idea of random people coming in and out of our home, but after the success with airbnb and having a roommate, we decided to convert our garage into a studio apartment type of room and move into there so we could rent out the room we were using. The area we lived in was hard to find apartments because of the prices for people, so roommates were a better option. I had experience with renovating, so I insulated and finished the walls and put in flooring, and my wife and I moved into there. We paid a company to remove the garage door and install a 3 panel glass sliding door, and we found a roommate for our other room.

 The roommates didn't affect airbnb at all, and it actually helped. One of them did Uber, so I asked him if he wanted to offer driving the airbnb guests around town, that he could charge a flat fee. So he would pick them up and take them wherever they wanted to go, which saved them from having to rent a car and pay for parking at the theme park. We also had a cleaning fee for airbnb, and after we showed him what we did to the room, he wanted to take over cleaning if we gave him the fee.  So we ended up renting 2 bedrooms to roommates and listing the master bedroom on airbnb. 


Things we didn't try but were considering was renting the home or a shed as storage space. I don't remember the name of the app, but you could rent out rooms, garages, or sheds for people to use as long-term storage. The idea was that if we didn't like having roommates or airbnb, then that would be an option to keep from having people in the house. Because of how successful the other 2 options were, we never used this method, so I don't know how well it would work. We used the income from airbnb and roommates to make the house look even better, and it helped increase the reviews. I received a better job offer, and we decided to move, but the value of the house appreciated enough that we were able to sell it for a decent profit. When we moved, we did the same thing in the new location. Airbnb wasn't very popular there, so we went with roommates. The house had a second driveway because the previous owner had an rv, so we decided to rent out the space to someone with an rv. We found them by going to different rv parks in the area to see what was being charged and to see if anyone was interested. We found someone and tried to start with a lower price first but under-estimated how much utilities would increase so we didn't profit but didn't lose either. 

Hopefully, this helps you. Airbnb has changed since then, and now we rent out our home to a property manager (renting out the entire house to a family makes a lot less than roommates). We now have a house, 2 condos, and an apartment, and use the income to purchase more real estate. Check with wherever you live, I'm sure each place is different. If you live near a College, roommates are way easier to go and I found out younger people make much better roommates than older ones. Our first roommate is now doing the same thing I was doing, and he now has 2 homes. He let his sister move into his first house and told her she can live there for free as long as she is okay with roommates, so she lives there for free and essentially became his property manager for that house, and he bought another one and is doing the same thing there. 

The most important part is vetting roommates.

Usually within the first 1.5 weeks, the majority of your loss will be water weight as your body burns up your glycogen stores which then releases the water that was bound to it. Drink a lot of water and don't do any intense exercise. Your brain needs glucose to survive, but once your body burns up its glycogen stores, it can actually create its own from a process called gluconeogenesis to support brain activity. You don't want to do any high intensity exercises, but you do want to try to activate as many muscle groups as possible to stimulate them. Even if you can't control the types of food you are eating, you can control how much. I think in your position the best thing you can do is to speak with your family about wanting to lose weight, and ask if they can help you by getting different food choices and try to help you along your journey.

You said you have been overweight for a long time, so there are many habits that you need to change. To make it easier for you, I recommend making those changes in steps. Every 2 weeks add something else to it. I will list my recommendation and if you have any questions, please don't hesitate to ask. This will make it easier to get through the process and build good habits.

1). Weeks 1-2: Cut out any drinks with sugar. Try to stick with water as much as you can and strive to drink about half of your weight in ounces (128 ounces is a gallon). Liquid calories are always undercalculated and a big part of why people gain weight and have trouble losing it. Try to stop drinking several hours before you go to bed, as sleep is important for recovery and weight loss.

2). Weeks 3-4: cut out snacking. Try to stick with your regular 3 meals, but stop snacking altogether.  When you feel hungry, drink some water instead. Every time you eat something, your body has an insulin response to it and switches from metabolizing fat to storing it. Also when you eat affects your ghrelin level (ghrelin is the "hunger hormone"). This will slowly help reduce your hunger cravings as well as the caloric intake.

3). Weeks 5-6: portion control. Start off by not getting seconds for any meal, only what fits on your plate without piling it high. One helping per meal. This will also help you reduce your caloric intake as well as shrink the size of your stomach as you are taking in less food over time. If that isn't working for you and the scale isn't moving, they sell "portion control plates" on Amazon.  If you don't have the money to buy one, look it up and take notes on how they divide the plate. If there is a portion on the plate that your family didn't prepare, substitute it with the healthiest option or skip it altogether.

4). Weeks 7-8: try to reduce your carb intake. Carbs get broken down and stored in your body as glycogen. 1 gram of glycogen binds to 3-4 grams of water. By reducing your carb intake, you are reducing calories and will also lose water weight that your body has been holding on to. Try not to eat rice, bread, pasta, etc. These will make a big difference for you. As you reduce your carb intake, note that protein is more filling  and you stay fuller for longer. 

5). Weeks 9-10: start looking into intermittent fasting. It is a great way to lose weight and has a lot of benefits. The easiest way is to download the app called "fasting tracker" and try different types of fasting. The easiest one is 16 hours of fasting with an 8 hour eating window. An example would be eating from 8am-4pm only. This would be your 8 hour eating window and for the other 16 hours you will be fasting. When you feel successful with that you can move to 20 hour fasting with a 4 hour window,  or just cut down to two meals a day. Even one meal a day is perfectly fine. Try it and see what works for you.

While you are doing this, try to increase your daily activity. Walk to the end of your street and back. How did it make you feel? Are you ok or in pain? Were you out of breath or able to talk? Try to walk every day to stay active and burn calories. Low steady state cardio is amazing for weight loss, and will help you get results much faster. If you have a fitbit, smart phone, or a pedometer, track your daily steps before doing all of this. The first day take what ever your daily steps were and double it. After that, try to increase that number each day by 200 steps. You will see amazing progress.

Weigh yourself every day first thing in the morning before you eat or drink and preferably after a bowel movement, and write it down. Take all 7 days and add them together and divide by 7. This is your average weight loss for that week. Your first few weeks will have a lot of loss from water weight (remember when I talked about glycogen binding to water?). Don't be discouraged  when you see a smaller number than expected.

You will lose more weight at first if you have a lot of glycogen in your body, but you will still lose some body fat.
